```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(mysterynpi)
```

Version 0.10.0 added three things that change what callers can do without
changing what any existing call returns: a selectable missing-data policy, an
input layer that accepts more shapes and says what each conversion costs, and a
result object with methods. Each exists because a standard asked for it (this
is the appendix the rOpenSci statistical standards work produced, assessed in
`srr/standards-compliance.md`), but each is useful on its own terms, and none
of them was documented for users until now.

## 1. Missing values: absence is not disagreement

Every agreement rule takes `na_action`.

```{r}
surname_agreement("SMITH", NA)
```

The default scores a missing value `"uninformative"`: absence of evidence, not
evidence of difference. This is the behaviour of every release before 0.10.0
and it is the whole reason the package exists, so it is the default and the
contract asserters run against it.

What is new is that you can ask for something louder.

```{r}
withCallingHandlers(
  surname_agreement("SMITH", NA, na_action = "warn"),
  warning = function(w) { message("warned: ", conditionMessage(w)); invokeRestart("muffleWarning") }
)
```

```{r, error = TRUE}
surname_agreement("SMITH", NA, na_action = "error")
```

Note that the rules differ in what they take. `surname_agreement()` compares
name strings, while `middle_agreement()` compares **token lists** from
`middle_tokens()` and `license_agreement()` takes a number and a state for each
side. `middle_tokens()` absorbs both a logical `NA` and an `NA_character_`, so
either reaches the rule as an empty token list and scores `"uninformative"`:

```{r}
middle_agreement(middle_tokens("ANNE"), middle_tokens(NA_character_))
license_agreement("12345", "CO", NA_character_, "CO")
```

`"warn"` reports once per call rather than once per row, so a 50,000-row
comparison gives you one warning with a count instead of a scroll. `"error"`
refuses before any comparison is made. Use `"error"` when a missing name in
your input means an upstream extraction failed and you would rather stop than
quietly score the pair as uninformative.

The same parameter is on all eight rules: `surname_agreement()`,
`given_name_agreement()`, `middle_agreement()`, `suffix_agreement()`,
`gender_agreement()`, `license_agreement()`, `nickname_agreement()` and
`graduation_year_agreement()`.

### Imputation is not offered, and that is deliberate

The statistical standards ask for an imputation option (`G2.14c`). This package
refuses it. An imputed name is a fabricated identity claim. The package exists
because absence of evidence was once read as evidence of difference; reading it
as evidence of *sameness* is worse, because it resolves a match on a name
nobody recorded. It is refused on the numeric graduation-year scale too, where
it would at least be well defined, because imputing a year manufactures the
very compatibility `graduation_year_agreement()` is asked to judge.

### Undefined is not missing

`NaN` and the infinities are arithmetic that went wrong upstream, not a value
nobody recorded, so they are handled separately.

```{r}
is_undefined_number(c(1, NA, NaN, Inf, -Inf))
finite_or_na(c(1, NaN, Inf))
```

`graduation_year_agreement()` takes its own `undefined` parameter for the same
reason: a year of `Inf` is a bug in whatever produced it, and you may want to
hear about it even when you are content for a missing year to be silent.

## 2. Input shapes: converted once, at the boundary, out loud

`match_npi()` now coerces its inputs through one layer rather than letting each
rule meet whatever it is handed.

```{r}
as_linkage_table(matrix(c("A", "B"), nrow = 1, dimnames = list(NULL, c("x", "y"))))
```

Accepted: `data.frame`, `tbl_df`, `data.table`, and a matrix with column names.
A matrix without column names is refused, because "you name the columns, we
never guess" is the package's input contract and an unnamed matrix has nothing
to name.

The conversions report what they cost, which is the point rather than noise:

```{r}
x <- read_name_column(factor(c("SMITH", "JONES")), nm = "last_name")
x
```

```{r}
y <- tryCatch(read_name_column(c(1234567890, 1234567891), nm = "npi"),
              warning = function(w) { message("warned: ", conditionMessage(w)); NULL })
```

That warning is the one worth reading. A numeric identifier loses leading
zeros and can round, and `as.character(1234567890)` on a larger value yields
`"1.23e+09"`, which then matches nothing. Read identifiers as character
upstream; the package warns rather than silently producing a column that cannot
match.

Two more refusals, both deliberate:

```{r, error = TRUE}
reject_list_columns(data.frame(id = 1, nm = I(list(c("A", "B")))))
```

```{r, error = TRUE}
check_scalar(c(1, 2), "seed")
```

A list column would stringify into a comparison as the literal text
`c("A", "B")` and conflict with every real name. A multi-valued `seed` or
`entity_filter` used to be silently truncated to its first element.

## 3. The result object

`match_npi()` returns an `npi_match_result`. **The class is additive**: the same
five elements under the same names as before, so every existing caller keeps
working, and `result$matches` is still a data frame.

What is new is that printing one is readable, and that the summary is a value
rather than text you have to parse:

```r
res <- match_npi(roster, table = "nppes")

res                      # six lines of summary, not every matched row
nobs(res)                # roster rows submitted
s <- summary(res)
s$statistics             # statistic / value / denominator
s$columns                # class, storage mode and missing count per column
```

`summary()` takes `digits` (default 3) and so do `print()` and `format()`, so
screen output does not change with your `options(digits)`. `s$statistics`
carries a `denominator` column, which names what each share was computed over:
a share without its denominator is the kind of number that gets quoted out of
context.

**There is no `plot()` method, on purpose.** A plot of a three-valued verdict
table is a bar chart of counts that `summary()` already reports more precisely,
and the one genuinely visual question here, which pairs a human should look at,
is answered by `clerical_sample()` rather than by a chart.
